common_name: Kozu Spice Calanthe (Discolor × Izu-insularis Hardy Woodland Orchid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich woodland soil in deep shade; mulch heavily where winters drop below USDA zone 7.

directions: Kozu Spice is a vigorous seed-grown garden strain resulting from crossing Calanthe discolor with the rare Izu Islands species Calanthe izu-insularis, bred originally for Japanese flower shows and later introduced to North American gardeners through specialty nurseries. Plant divisions in spring into consistently moist, humus-rich woodland soil in deep shade, where the broad pleated leaves form a slowly spreading evergreen groundcover. In mid-spring each clump sends up clusters of clove-scented flowers that vary seedling to seedling in bicolor combinations of white, yellow, and red. Mulch heavily in regions colder than USDA zone 7 to protect the crowns through winter, since foliage damage begins below about 10°F.
sources: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Takane Calanthe (Sieboldii × Discolor Hardy Woodland Orchid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in leaf-mold-enriched woodland soil in light to full shade; mulch for winter outside the warm end of its range.

directions: Takane is a Japanese seed strain combining Calanthe sieboldii with Calanthe discolor, chosen for its multicolored spring flowers and tidy, tropical-looking foliage clumps. Set divisions in light shade to full shade in woodland soil enriched with leaf mold, where the pleated evergreen leaves stay attractive through the growing season. Flower stalks rise above the foliage in mid-spring carrying blooms that blend yellow, orange, and apricot tones, giving each clump a warm, multicolored effect distinct from the more common white- or pink-flowered Calanthe hybrids. Winter protection with a thick mulch layer is recommended outside the warmer end of its hardiness range.

planting.note: Plant pseudobulbs shallowly in spring in humus-rich, sharply drained soil in partial shade to avoid winter rhizome rot.

directions: Kuchi-beni, Japanese for 'red lips,' is a selection of the hardy ground orchid Bletilla striata chosen for flowers that are mostly soft white with a vivid pink-to-violet blush concentrated at the tip of the lip. Plant the flattened pseudobulbs shallowly in spring in humus-rich, sharply drained soil in partial shade, since waterlogged winter soil is the most common cause of rhizome rot in this otherwise easy species. Clumps send up slender flowering stems in late spring bearing the two-toned blooms above pleated, lance-shaped foliage. Established plantings slowly multiply by offset pseudobulbs and benefit from division every few years once crowded.

common_name: First Kiss Bletilla (White-Edged Leaf Hardy Ground Orchid)

planting.note: Plant pseudobulb divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; mulch for winter at the cold end of its range.

directions: First Kiss is a foliage-selected cultivar of the hardy ground orchid Bletilla striata, distinguished by a crisp white margin along the edges of its long, pleated green leaves. Plant pseudobulb divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade, where the variegated foliage emerges in late March ahead of the flowering stems. In late spring, stems rise above the leaves bearing white flowers lightly blushed with purple, offering a softer color combination than the species' typical magenta-pink. The cultivar is reliably hardy through USDA zone 6 with winter mulch and spreads gradually into a fuller clump over several seasons.
sources: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Penway Paris Bletilla (Giant Pink Hardy Ground Orchid Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, allowing extra room for its larger ultimate size.

directions: Penway Paris is a vigorous interspecific hybrid bred in the UK by combining Bletilla striata with its Taiwanese relative, producing a notably larger plant than either parent, with flowering stems that can top three feet in good conditions. Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, giving this hybrid more room than standard Bletilla striata because of its larger ultimate size. Pale pink flowers open along the tall stems in late spring, each marked with fine purple streaking on a yellow lip that contrasts against the surrounding petals. Winter mulch is advisable outside the milder end of its hardiness range to protect the shallow pseudobulbs from freeze-thaw damage.

common_name: Farges' Lady's Slipper Orchid (Mottled-Leaf Chinese Cypripedium)

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in partial shade in gritty, humus-rich soil that drains freely during the winter dormant rest.

directions: Cypripedium fargesii is a dwarf Chinese lady's slipper grown chiefly for its broad, rounded leaves heavily marked with blackish-brown mottling, a pattern it shares with its close relative C. lichiangense. Plant divisions or nursery-grown starts in partial shade in gritty, humus-rich soil that stays evenly moist through the growing season but drains freely enough to avoid standing water during the dormant winter rest. In mid-spring short stems barely clearing the foliage carry a single yellowish-green flower spotted with maroon, with a yellow, red-spotted lip and a dark maroon staminode. This species is slower to establish and more particular about drainage than the common North American lady's slippers, rewarding patient growers with an unusually patterned bloom rarely seen in cultivation.
